Area.evidence_source: The current study ofers novel insights about the interplaying dynamics of suicidality among a diverse group of GB2SM. Echoing the fndings of other research (D'Augelli & Grossman, 2001; Diaz et al., 2001; Ferlatte et al., 2015; Irwin et al., 2014; Paget et al., 2016; Plöderl et al., 2013, 2014; Salway et al., 2018), the participants' narratives were replete with descriptions of adverse childhood events including abuse and violence, which they linked to their suicidality. These challenges were deeply enmeshed with other critical moments across their histories and were often manifested in the 'spiraling down without capital' and eventual 'social isolation' key themes in the analysis. In describing their struggles over identity, upbringing, personhood, place as well as sexuality, the participants revealed the ways in which 'risk factors' are a product of multiple aspects of the person, and fundamentally challenge sexuality as the 'catch all' determinant of suicidality among GB2SM. This is not to diminish the centrality of sexual identity and homophobia in the production of sufering and suicidality. Rather, the fndings outlined in this article suggest a view of suicidality as complex and produced by multiple and intertwined factors and forms of domination (including homophobia, classism, sexism, racism, mental health stigma), rather than the outcome of a singular and independent factor. Building on this, the importance of considering the lifecourse of GB2SM in suicide research was evident whereby long-standing struggles and difculties that predated adulthood featured prominently in the narratives of participants. The life-course dimension of suicidality refects the importance of embedding seemingly disparate 'events' related to suicidality within a broader process of becoming—rather than being—'suicidal' (Blackman, 2012). In essence, formative moments and normative infuences haunted (Gordon, 2008) the participants and often assembled in highly problematic ways to tip them in the direction of suicide. That is, not only is suicidality uniquely multifactorial, but it is also temporally bound. A focus on the process of becoming thereby reveals suicidality as inextricably linked in a historicity of intersecting factors. Such dynamics refect many of the logics espoused previously in work on intersectionality, but that have hitherto not been incorporate in suicidality work. The current fndings also highlight the particular ways in which limits or losses of fnancial capital contribute to suicidality among GB2SM. Indeed, other studies have found that a disproportionate number of sexual minorities are living in poverty (Lee Badgett, Durso, & Schneebaum, 2013; Ross et al., 2016). In conclusion, suicidality among GB2SM is the result of a constellation of factors beyond sexuality. After all, GB2SM are also 'classed,' 'gendered' and 'raced,', and as such, they are vulnerable to other forms of structural violence including classism, sexism and racism.
